sites.name: Apostolic council of Jerusalem
sites.summary: Meeting of Paul and Barnabas with James, Peter and John over whether gentile converts must be circumcised. Acts presents a decree requiring only abstention from idol-meat, blood, strangled animals and fornication; Paul's own account in Galatians differs, and the Antioch incident followed.

sites.name: Council of Carthage on rebaptism
sites.summary: On 1 September 256, 87 African bishops under Cyprian voted one by one (the Sententiae episcoporum survive) that converts baptised by heretics or schismatics must be rebaptised, defying Pope Stephen. The precedent later underpinned Donatist theology.

sites.name: Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata
sites.summary: Bishops deposed Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch and a ducenarius in Zenobia's service, for adoptionist teaching and worldly display. Paul refused to leave the church house; after recovering Antioch, Aurelian ruled in 272 that it belonged to whomever the bishops of Italy and Rome recognised, the first imperial ruling in an internal church dispute.

sites.name: Synod of Rome under Miltiades
sites.summary: Constantine's first intervention in church affairs: Pope Miltiades with three Gallic and fifteen Italian bishops met in Fausta's house on the Lateran from 2 October 313 and acquitted Caecilian of Carthage. The Donatists appealed, leading to Arles.

sites.name: Council of Arles
sites.summary: Summoned by Constantine for 1 August 314, attended by some 33 bishops from Gaul, Britain, Spain, Italy and Africa. It rejected the Donatist appeal and issued 22 canons, including excommunication of soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.

sites.name: Council of Ancyra
sites.summary: Eastern bishops met after Maximinus Daia's death to set penances for those who lapsed in the persecution; its 25 canons include rules on clergy who sacrificed under torture and on bestiality.

sites.name: Council of Nicaea
sites.summary: Constantine's council, opened c. 20 May 325 in the palace at Nicaea, with some 250-300 bishops (tradition: 318). It condemned Arius, adopted a creed defining the Son as homoousios with the Father, fixed a common Easter date and ranked Alexandria, Antioch and Rome. Constantine paid for the bishops' travel by public post.

sites.name: Council of Tyre
sites.summary: Eusebian bishops deposed Athanasius on charges of violence against Melitians, including the murder of Arsenius, who was produced alive. Constantine exiled Athanasius to Trier anyway after he allegedly threatened to stop the Egyptian grain fleet.

sites.name: Dedication Council of Antioch
sites.summary: Some 97 bishops met at the dedication of Constantine's Golden Octagon in the presence of Constantius II and issued creeds avoiding homoousios, and 25 canons long used in both East and West.

sites.name: Council of Gangra
sites.summary: Anatolian bishops condemned the followers of Eustathius of Sebaste for extreme asceticism: rejecting marriage, encouraging slaves to leave masters and women to cut their hair and wear men's clothes. The date is disputed (c. 340-355).

sites.name: Council of Serdica
sites.summary: Called by Constans and Constantius II to reunite East and West; the Easterners refused to sit with Athanasius, withdrew to Philippopolis and excommunicated Pope Julius. The Westerners' canons gave Rome a role in appeals by deposed bishops.

sites.name: Council of Sirmium (the "Blasphemy")
sites.summary: A small council with Constantius II present issued a creed forbidding the terms ousia, homoousios and homoiousios; Hilary called it the 'blasphemy'. Ossius of Corduba and Pope Liberius were pressured into signing.

sites.name: Council of Ariminum
sites.summary: Over 400 Western bishops, detained at Ariminum until they signed, accepted a Homoian creed ('the Son is like the Father'), prompting Jerome's line that 'the whole world groaned and was amazed to find itself Arian'.

sites.name: Council of Seleucia in Isauria
sites.summary: The Eastern half of Constantius' twin council, held from 27 September 359 with about 160 bishops, split between Homoiousians and Homoians; delegates were then made to sign the Homoian creed at Constantinople.

sites.name: Council of Alexandria
sites.summary: Athanasius, back under Julian's amnesty, held a small synod whose Tome to the Antiochenes accepted different terminologies for the Trinity, preparing the Nicene reconciliation of 381.

sites.name: Council of Laodicea
sites.summary: Phrygian synod of uncertain date (c. 363-364) whose 60 canons ban Christians from keeping the Jewish Sabbath, celebrating with Jews, and wearing amulets, and include an early list of canonical books.

sites.name: First Council of Constantinople
sites.summary: Theodosius I's council of about 150 Eastern bishops reaffirmed Nicaea against Arians and Pneumatomachians, produced (or endorsed) the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed, ranked Constantinople second after Rome, and saw Gregory of Nazianzus resign as bishop.

sites.name: Council of Aquileia
sites.summary: Ambrose, with Gratian's support, conducted a hostile examination of the Homoian bishops Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum and deposed them; the stenographic minutes survive.

sites.name: Council of Hippo
sites.summary: African plenary council at which Augustine, still a priest, spoke on the creed; it issued a list of canonical scriptures including the deuterocanonical books, reaffirmed at Carthage in 397.

sites.name: Synod of Isaac (Seleucia-Ctesiphon)
sites.summary: With Yazdegerd I's permission and the help of the Roman envoy Marutha of Maypherqat, the Persian bishops accepted Nicaea and organised the Church of the East under the catholicos Isaac, independent of Antioch.

sites.name: Conference of Carthage
sites.summary: Honorius' commissioner Marcellinus presided over a three-day hearing between 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops, whose roll-call records over 400 African sees. He ruled for the Catholics, and the edict of 412 outlawed Donatism.

sites.name: Synod of Diospolis
sites.summary: Fourteen Palestinian bishops acquitted Pelagius of heresy after he disowned the propositions charged against him; Augustine and the African church responded by securing his condemnation by Pope Innocent I in 417.

sites.name: Council of Ephesus
sites.summary: Cyril of Alexandria opened the council on 22 June 431 before the Antiochene bishops arrived, deposed Nestorius and proclaimed Mary Theotokos; John of Antioch's rival assembly deposed Cyril. Theodosius II eventually sided with Cyril; the reunion formula of 433 patched the split.

sites.name: Second Council of Ephesus (Latrocinium)
sites.summary: Dioscorus of Alexandria, backed by Theodosius II, rehabilitated Eutyches and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough handling; Leo I's Tome was not read. Leo called it a robbery (latrocinium).

sites.name: Council of Chalcedon
sites.summary: Marcian's council of some 370 bishops, met from 8 October 451 in the church of St Euphemia, deposed Dioscorus, accepted Leo's Tome and defined Christ 'in two natures'. Canon 28 gave Constantinople equal privileges with Rome. The definition split the Eastern churches permanently: Egypt and much of Syria and Armenia rejected it.

sites.name: Councils of Dvin
sites.summary: Armenian church councils at the Persian-Armenian capital: the first (505/506) condemned the Church of the East's Nestorianism and accepted Zeno's Henotikon; the second (554) broke with Chalcedon, separating the Armenian church from Constantinople.

sites.name: Council of Agde
sites.summary: Thirty-five bishops of Visigothic Gaul under Caesarius of Arles met with Alaric II's permission months before Vouillé; its 47 canons on clergy, church property and penance became a reference collection.

sites.name: First Council of Orléans
sites.summary: Clovis' council of 32 bishops of the Frankish kingdom, held weeks before his death, set rules for church asylum, the ordination of slaves and royal control over making clergy.

sites.name: Second Council of Constantinople
sites.summary: Justinian's council condemned the Three Chapters (Theodore of Mopsuestia and writings of Theodoret and Ibas) to placate anti-Chalcedonians. Pope Vigilius, held in Constantinople, first refused then submitted; northern Italian sees went into schism.

sites.name: Third Council of Toledo
sites.summary: King Reccared and his Gothic nobles renounced Arianism before 62 bishops on 8 May 589, unifying the Visigothic kingdom with its Hispano-Roman Catholic majority. The council's creed included the Filioque.

sites.name: Monastery of St Antony (Inner Mountain)
sites.summary: Antony (c. 251-356) withdrew to a fort at Pispir on the Nile and then to the 'Inner Mountain' near the Red Sea, where disciples settled around him. Athanasius' Life of Antony (c. 360), quickly translated into Latin, made him the model of the hermit and helped convert Augustine.

sites.name: Nitria
sites.summary: Founded by Amoun c. 325 at the edge of the natron desert. Palladius found some 5,000 monks living here c. 390, with seven bakeries, doctors and a church; whips hung from palm trees for punishing offenders. Rufinus, Melania the Elder and Evagrius all passed through.

sites.name: Kellia
sites.summary: 'The Cells', founded c. 338 by Amoun and Antony for monks wanting more solitude than Nitria offered; Evagrius Ponticus lived here 385-399. Excavations since 1964 have mapped over 1,500 hermitages across 100 km2.

sites.name: Scetis (Wadi Natrun)
sites.summary: Desert valley settled by Macarius the Egyptian c. 330, home of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum). Sacked by Mazices raiders in 407, 434 and 444. Four monasteries survive in continuous use.

sites.name: Tabennisi and Pbow (Pachomian koinonia)
sites.summary: Pachomius, a former conscript, founded the first communal monastery at Tabennisi c. 323 and the headquarters at Pbow; by his death in 346 there were nine houses with several thousand monks under a written rule, organised by trades, with twice-yearly assemblies. Jerome translated the rule in 404. The Nag Hammadi codices were found nearby.

sites.name: White Monastery (Atripe)
sites.summary: Shenoute of Atripe (abbot c. 385-465) ruled a federation of some 4,000 monks and nuns, built the great church of c. 440, and led raids smashing pagan shrines; his Coptic writings are the core of Coptic literature.

sites.name: Lérins
sites.summary: Island monastery founded by Honoratus c. 410, a nursery of bishops for 5th-century Gaul: Hilary and Caesarius of Arles, Eucherius of Lyon, Lupus of Troyes, Faustus of Riez. Vincent of Lérins wrote his Commonitorium (434) here.

sites.name: Ligugé
sites.summary: Martin, former cavalry officer, founded this hermitage near Poitiers c. 361 under Hilary's patronage, the earliest known monastery in Gaul.

sites.name: Marmoutier
sites.summary: Monastery founded by Martin across the Loire from Tours after he became bishop: some 80 monks lived in caves and wooden cells, with no property, eating together, and copying books.

sites.name: Saint-Victor, Marseille
sites.summary: Founded c. 415 by John Cassian, who had lived in Egypt; his Institutes and Conferences transmitted Egyptian monasticism to the West and were prescribed reading in Benedict's Rule.

sites.name: Condat (Saint-Claude)
sites.summary: Founded c. 435 in the Jura by the brothers Romanus and Lupicinus; the Life of the Jura Fathers describes a growing network of houses and a rule combining Eastern and Lérinian models.

sites.name: Agaune (Saint-Maurice)
sites.summary: Shrine of the Theban Legion, whose martyrdom under Maximian Eucherius of Lyon narrated c. 440. In 515 the Burgundian prince Sigismund founded a monastery with the laus perennis, continuous chant by rotating choirs, the oldest continuously occupied abbey in the West.

sites.name: Monte Cassino
sites.summary: Benedict of Nursia founded the monastery c. 529 on the site of a temple of Apollo and wrote his Rule here. Gregory the Great's Dialogues (Book 2) narrate his life. Lombards sacked it c. 577-581; the monks fled to Rome with the autograph Rule.

sites.name: Subiaco
sites.summary: Benedict lived as a hermit in a cave (Sacro Speco) near Nero's dammed lakes at Subiaco c. 500-529 and founded twelve small monasteries before moving to Monte Cassino.

sites.name: Vivarium
sites.summary: Cassiodorus, retired from Ostrogothic service, founded Vivarium on his estate at Squillace with fishponds, baths and a scriptorium. His Institutions laid out a programme of sacred and secular reading and copying that shaped monastic libraries; its books reached the Lateran and Bobbio.

sites.name: Castellum Lucullanum
sites.summary: Lucullus' old villa at Naples, where the deposed Romulus Augustulus was pensioned off in 476. Severinus of Noricum's body was brought here c. 492 and a monastery founded, where Eugippius wrote the Life of Severinus and compiled excerpts of Augustine.

sites.name: Mar Saba (Great Lavra)
sites.summary: Lavra founded in 483 by Sabas in the Kidron gorge; Sabas led the Palestinian monks in support of Chalcedon. Persian-era raiders killed 44 monks in 614. Cyril of Scythopolis wrote the Lives of the Palestinian monks.

sites.name: Monastery of St Catherine, Sinai
sites.summary: Justinian fortified the monastery at the Burning Bush between 548 and 565, as dated by inscriptions on the church roof beams; Egeria had visited monks here in 383/4. Its apse mosaic of the Transfiguration and the pre-iconoclast icons, including the Christ Pantokrator, are unique survivals.

sites.name: Mor Gabriel (Qartmin)
sites.summary: Syriac monastery in Tur Abdin founded in 397, said to have received endowments from Arcadius and Theodosius II; Anastasius funded its great church in 512. Still active.

sites.name: Iona
sites.summary: Founded by the Irish prince-monk Columba in 563; from here missions went to the Picts and, in 635, Aidan to Northumbria. Adomnán's Life of Columba (c. 700) describes the community.

sites.name: Whithorn (Candida Casa)
sites.summary: Bede says Ninian built a stone church here dedicated to Martin, called 'the white house'. The Latinus stone (c. 450) is the earliest Christian memorial in Scotland.

sites.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
sites.summary: Constantine ordered Hadrian's temple of Venus removed in 326 to expose the rock tomb of Christ, and built a basilica (the Martyrium) and the rotunda of the Anastasis, dedicated in 335. The legend of Helena's discovery of the True Cross appears by the 390s. Egeria (384) describes the liturgy; the Persians took the Cross in 614 and Heraclius restored it in 630.

sites.name: Abu Mena
sites.summary: Shrine of the soldier-martyr Menas in the Mareotis, which grew into a pilgrim town with a great basilica under Arcadius and Zeno, baths, inns, and workshops making the clay flasks for holy water stamped with Menas between two camels, found from Marseille to Britain.

sites.name: Tomb of Martin at Tours
sites.summary: Martin died in 397 and was buried outside Tours. Bishop Perpetuus built a large basilica c. 470; Clovis came here after Vouillé (507) and received the consular insignia. Gregory of Tours recorded hundreds of miracles at the tomb.

sites.name: Qal'at Sim'an
sites.summary: Simeon the Stylite lived on a column here from c. 423 until his death in 459, preaching to pilgrims from Gaul to Persia. Zeno's government built around the column a cross-shaped martyrium of four basilicas (c. 476-490), the largest church in the East before Hagia Sophia.

sites.name: Sergiopolis (Resafa)
sites.summary: Desert fort where the soldier-martyr Sergius was buried. Anastasius renamed it Sergiopolis and Justinian walled it; the saint was venerated by Arab tribes and by Khosrow II, who sent gold crosses after his restoration in 591.

sites.name: Hagios Demetrios, Thessalonica
sites.summary: Basilica of the city's soldier-saint, rebuilt after a fire c. 620. The Miracles of St Demetrius credit him with defending the city from the Avar and Slav sieges of 586 and 615-618.

sites.name: Basilica of St John, Ephesus
sites.summary: Shrine on the Ayasoluk hill over the tomb of John the Evangelist, rebuilt by Justinian and Theodora as a domed cross basilica. The Seven Sleepers' cave nearby drew pilgrims after their 'awakening' in the reign of Theodosius II.

sites.name: Shrine of Felix at Nola (Cimitile)
sites.summary: Paulinus, a senator and consul, gave away his fortune and settled at the tomb of the confessor Felix c. 395, building a basilica complex and writing annual poems on the saint's feast; bishop of Nola 409-431.

sites.name: Tomb of Peter (Vatican necropolis)
sites.summary: The presbyter Gaius (c. 200) said he could show 'the trophies of the apostles' on the Vatican and the Ostian Way; excavations of 1940-49 found a small aedicula of c. 160 in a pagan cemetery, over which Constantine built Old St Peter's by cutting into the hill.

sites.name: Catacomb of Callixtus
sites.summary: The first official cemetery of the Roman church, administered by the deacon Callixtus under Zephyrinus. Its 'Crypt of the Popes' holds the tombs of nine 3rd-century bishops; Pope Sixtus II, seized while preaching in a nearby cemetery and beheaded with four deacons in 258, was buried here. Damasus decorated it with verse inscriptions.

sites.name: Martyrs of Lyon
sites.summary: In 177 a mob and the governor tortured and killed about 48 Christians in the amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, including the slave Blandina, who outlasted everyone, the deacon Sanctus and the old bishop Pothinus; their ashes were thrown into the Rhône.

sites.name: Martyrdoms of Carthage (Perpetua, Cyprian)
sites.summary: The young noblewoman Perpetua, whose prison diary survives, and the slave Felicity died in the amphitheatre on 7 March 203 at games for Geta's birthday. Cyprian was beheaded at the Ager Sexti on 14 September 258; his Proconsular Acts record the trial.

sites.name: Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
sites.summary: Forty soldiers of legio XII Fulminata were left to freeze on a frozen lake near Sebaste c. 320 under Licinius. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa preached on them and their relics spread across the East.

sites.name: Shrine of Thecla, Seleucia (Meryemlik)
sites.summary: Cave shrine of Paul's legendary female disciple Thecla south of Seleucia, visited by Egeria in 384, who found monks and virgins there; Zeno built a great basilica in thanks for regaining his throne (476).

sites.name: Shrine of Cyrus and John at Menouthis
sites.summary: Cyril of Alexandria moved the relics of the martyrs Cyrus and John here c. 414 to supplant a popular healing shrine of Isis; Sophronius of Jerusalem later recorded 70 miracles. The site is now under Abukir Bay.

sites.name: Shrine of Alban at Verulamium
sites.summary: Britain's protomartyr, a citizen of Verulamium beheaded for sheltering a priest, under Decius or Diocletian. Germanus of Auxerre visited the tomb in 429; Gildas and Bede tell the story. The abbey stands on the hill of execution.

sites.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis
sites.summary: Genovefa built a church over Denis' tomb north of Paris c. 475; the Merovingian queen Arnegundis (d. c. 580) was buried there, and Dagobert I made it the royal abbey.

sites.name: Shrine of Eulalia at Emerita
sites.summary: The twelve-year-old Eulalia, burned in 304, became the patron of Lusitania; Prudentius wrote her hymn, and Hydatius credits her with the drowning of the Suevic king Hermigarius in the Guadiana after he insulted her in 429.

sites.name: Martyr cemetery of Manastirine, Salona
sites.summary: Cemetery outside Salona where Bishop Domnius and other Diocletianic martyrs were buried, the core of a basilica complex; the bishops of Salona were buried around them until the city fell to Avars and Slavs c. 614.

sites.name: Basilica of Crispina at Theveste
sites.summary: Crispina, a woman of Thagara, was beheaded at Theveste in December 304. A huge pilgrimage basilica with a monastery and hostels was built on her shrine in the late 4th century.

sites.name: Babylas at Daphne
sites.summary: Gallus Caesar moved the relics of Bishop Babylas (d. 250) to the grove of Apollo at Daphne c. 351. In 362 Julian had them removed because the oracle was silenced; days later the temple of Apollo burned, which pagans blamed on Christians and Christians on God.

sites.name: Wondrous Mountain of Simeon the Younger
sites.summary: Simeon Stylites the Younger stood on columns from childhood until 592; the monastery around his pillar southwest of Antioch drew pilgrims selling clay eulogia tokens stamped with his image.

sites.name: Edessa: Abgar's letter and the Mandylion
sites.summary: Egeria (384) was shown the gates through which Abgar's letter from Jesus had been carried, a letter that protected the city. Evagrius credits a miraculous image of Christ with saving Edessa from Khosrow I's siege of 544, the first mention of the Mandylion.

sites.name: Shrine of Julian at Brioude
sites.summary: Tomb of the soldier-martyr Julian, killed under Decius or Diocletian, Gaul's second shrine after Tours; the emperor Avitus was buried here in 456. Gregory of Tours wrote a book of his miracles.
